newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW-Wheelock sees rising recurrent.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Wheelock sees rising recurrent.

text.p: Conglomerate Wheelock and Co Ltd said on Tuesday it expected its recurrent profit to be slightly better in the 1996/97 fiscal year compared to the previous year, and better still in 1997/1998.

Managing director John Hung said in an interview he based his reasoning on continuing improvement in the company's various businesses, including property and telecommunications, which had dragged down earnings in the past two years.
"Now with both going better, obviously '97 we should see a better year, and '98 even better," he said.
The group posted operating profit of HK$195.1 million for the year to March 31, 1996, and booked operating profit of HK$166.6 million for the first half of 1996/97.
It posted net profit of HK$2.46 billion and HK$788 million respectively for 1995/96 and first half 1996/97 following contributions from subsidiaries and associates.
Wheelock is engaged in property, telecommunications, infrastructure, trading and retailing, and hotel management.
The company was benefitting from a recovery in the local real estate market late last year, after the doldrums that started in mid-1994, Hung said.

Following the launch of government measures in mid-1994 to cool down the overheated property market, prices had dropped 10 to 30 percent from their 1994 peaks. They have since rebounded about 30 percent from late 1995 lows.
"Property sales (by property arm Wheelock Properties Ltd) make the subisidiary very strong," Hung said.
The group will start replenishing its land bank when opportunities arise, he said.
Hong Kong investment commercial properties held by Wheelock's 46-percent-held Wharf (Holdings) Ltd, such as Times Square and Harbour City, were doing well, Hung said.
Times Square, for instance, was generating annual rental turnover of more than HK$1.0 billion compared with the HK$750 million projected when the development was built, he said.
Wheelock's property business in Singapore, run through 71.24-percent held subsidiary New Asia Realty and Trust Co Ltd , was also faring well, he said.
On the telecommunications side, Hung said Wharf's cable television unit Wharf Cable Ltd was on track to break even by the end of 1997, with more than 310,000 subscribers by the end of last year.
He noted Wheelock group had suffered from the cost of the investment in Wharf Cable and a slowdown of the local property market in the past two years.
"So the group is generally looking potentially much stronger than two years ago," Hung said.
Wheelock would also benefit from developments in other businesses, including infrastructure, Hung said.

The HK$7.5 billion Western Harbour Tunnel, owned by Cross-Harbour Tunnel Co Ltd in which Wharf has a 26.7 percent stake, will be opened in April ahead of the originally scheduled opening date in September, he said.
While its retail arm Lane Crawford International Ltd was expected to post a loss for the year to March 31, 1997, the unit had an "immaterial" effect on Wheelock's earnings, Hung said.
The retailer contributed only one percent to Wheelock's profit in the past two years, and only four percent at its highest ever around 1991/92, he said.
Wharf and New Asia are the biggest profit contributors for Wheelock, Hung said.
-- Carrie Lee, Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6590
